How the glass on this site works

A practical walkthrough of sampled backdrops, rounded rims, flipped reflections, and chromatic aberration—with two live rendering labs.

By Felipe de SotoOctober 5, 2026

The glass on my portfolio does more than blur a translucent rectangle. It samples the image behind a surface, bends that image around a rounded rim, mirrors a narrow strip at the boundary, and separates its red and blue channels. The browser still draws the text and buttons as ordinary HTML.

In this post, I follow one card from the DOM to the shader, explain the material and the rim math, and give you two labs that use the same WebGL renderer. You can change values, switch individual scene layers, and open either lab fullscreen. Nothing here needs a server or a database.

The local renderer adapts ybouane/liquidglass, an MIT-licensed library. My site's configuration and composition sit around that renderer; the cards use WebGL, while the animated landing-page ribbons use VGPU and WebGPU. These are related paths, with different jobs.

Try the material lab

Start by moving Chromatic aberration between zero and 0.4. Then turn Rim softness down to zero and compare the colored edges. Increasing Z-axis radius spreads the bevel; changing Glass color changes the added frost, rather than recoloring the source image itself.

The lab uses the production GlassRenderer and its GLSL functions. Its source scene is deliberately small: a canvas of shapes and sampled text, with a live HTML label above the glass. It does not run the portfolio's whole DOM capture system. This makes the shader easier to inspect without pretending the simplified backdrop is the complete page.

The lab's reset affects only this instance. Its controls do not change the portfolio's appearance settings or save a preference. If WebGL is unavailable, the lab identifies its CSS fallback; that fallback cannot reproduce the GPU's flipped reflections or color separation.

Keep the image and the interface separate

I think of each surface as two outputs: an image of what is behind it, and real content above it. The image can be distorted. The content needs to stay readable, selectable, focusable, and clickable.

CSS backdrop-filter supplies the native frosted fallback. It can blur and saturate the backdrop, but it does not implement this site's rounded refraction, mirrored border, or per-channel sample offsets. The GPU shader supplies those details when initialization succeeds.

A GPU canvas also cannot automatically read arbitrary DOM text behind it. The site builds a scene texture from the lighting canvas and cached foreground images. Those images are inputs for the visual effect, not replacements for the accessible page.

For example, the selected navigation pill sits above the native navigation labels. Its backdrop contains a cached image of those labels, so their pixels can bend through the lens. The links underneath remain real anchors. Text inside an ordinary content card is drawn above its glass image and stays sharp.

Follow one card through the pipeline

Here is the route from a .glass element to its visible result:

  1. Collect the surfaces. src/main.js asynchronously imports createGlassSurfaces from src/liquid-glass.js. Initialization waits for the fonts, finds .glass elements, and creates empty lenses in a shared scene.
  2. Build the backdrop. The lighting canvas becomes the scene's background. createGlassBackdrop in src/glass-backdrop.js adds ordered proxies for cards, page text, the header, and the live ribbon canvas.
  3. Read one material. createGlassMaterialCache in src/glass-settings.js reads the root CSS variables. Cards, navigation, and ribbons share that snapshot until a relevant style or viewport change invalidates it.
  4. Measure the surface. glassSceneGeometry and glassSurfaceView map its position, local dimensions, and optional hover transform to the sampled scene. The renderer also captures a margin around the surface for the rim's outward-looking samples.
  5. Shade the background. The adapted GlassRenderer uploads that crop, optionally blurs it, and draws the lens. The fragment shader computes refraction, channel separation, mirrored reflection, frost, and the surface mask.
  6. Put the canvas under live content. createGlassSurfaces moves the result into a .glass-render-layer inside the actual card. The card's text and controls remain HTML above it.

This excerpt is from the initialization call in src/liquid-glass.js:

instance = await LiquidGlass.init({
  root: scene,
  backgroundColor: getComputedStyle(document.documentElement).backgroundColor,
  glassElements: lenses.map(({ lens }) => lens),
  defaults: materials.read(),
  maxPixelRatio: 1,
  captureGlassContent: false,
});
instance.pause();

captureGlassContent: false keeps the vendor's content-copy path from drawing a second copy of the live card text. The separate backdrop system supplies foreground images where another lens needs to see them. pause() stops the vendor's perpetual loop; the site's scheduler requests rendering when the scene or geometry changes.

Scene layers are different from ribbon layers

The next lab has four independent scene switches. The background and sampled text build the scene. A rear glass pane samples that scene, then a front pane samples the result beneath it. Live HTML labels remain above the visual output.

Try disabling Sampled text while leaving both panes visible. Then enable it again and turn off the Rear glass pane. The front pane remains enabled, but the image available for it to refract changes. Switching off one layer does not switch off the others.

This is the same WebGL glass material with a controlled, canvas-composited scene. The sampled text stands in for the portfolio's cached foreground images; there is no repeated HTML screenshot in the lab. It demonstrates paint order, rather than reproducing every capture and hover rule on the CV.

On the portfolio, compareBackdropLayers in src/glass-backdrop.js orders page content, fixed header content, the draggable lens, and optional controls. Within a level, DOM order matters. Parents paint before nested glass. The navigation's clear pill can therefore sample both the bar beneath it and its cached labels.

The three procedural ribbons are a separate composition problem. In src/shader.js, a WGSL loop draws ribbon layers in reverse order, from back to front. Their completed canvas becomes one live foreground source for later page lenses. Three ribbons do not mean three DOM capture layers, and the layer lab does not toggle the ribbons.

One material, two kinds of blur

These are the portfolio's six main settings, as normalized in src/glass-settings.js. The demos use a local settings object with the same mappings.

Setting CSS property Site default What changes
Color amount --glass-color-amount 0.188, or 18.8% How much of the frost color mixes into the sampled image.
Glass color --glass-frost-rgb 79, 79, 79, or #4F4F4F The frost's color.
Blur --glass-blur-amount 0 The broad blur of the sampled surface.
Distortion --glass-distortion 4 The strength of the curved-rim sampling offsets.
Chromatic aberration --glass-chromatic-aberration 0.4 The separation between red and blue sample positions.
Z-axis radius --glass-depth 60 CSS px The width available for the rounded depth profile.

Color amount is not a second opacity applied to the completed canvas. The backdrop stays solid, and frost is mixed into it once. Fading the completed result would expose the undistorted background underneath and create a double image.

Additional properties in src/glass.css control the optical approximation:

Property Site default Role
--glass-thickness 24 CSS px The ray's travel through the rim, bounded by the bevel.
--glass-refraction-index 1.45 The index used by GLSL refract.
--glass-edge-reflection 0.85 The weight of the mirrored boundary sample.
--glass-reflection-blur 6 CSS px Maximum softness of rim reflections and chromatic fringes.
--glass-header-depth-scale 2 A broader bevel for navigation glass.
--glass-playground-depth-scale 2.5 A broader bevel for the draggable lens.

Full-surface blur and rim softness are independent. The first blurs the transmitted backdrop broadly. The second fades in only within the narrow boundary band. At zero full-surface blur, the center can stay clear while the reflected and color-separated edge samples soften.

The shader blurs each displaced channel around its own position. Red stays offset in one direction, blue in the other. It does not average the channels into one gray sample. Setting rim softness to zero restores the sharper samples; setting chromatic aberration to zero disables the extra softness on transmitted color samples while mirrored reflections can still be soft.

The selected navigation pill uses a clear variant: its frost amount is zero, but its refraction settings still come from the shared material. Matte defaults also leave specular highlights, Fresnel shine, and decorative borders disabled.

Build a rounded rim instead of warping the whole card

The card's boundary is described by a signed-distance function in src/vendor/liquidglass.js. Ordinary cards use a rounded rectangle; the draggable lens uses a quartic superellipse in XY. A separate quartic cross-section rounds the surface in Z.

For that depth profile, the conceptual cross-section is:

x⁴ + z⁴ = 1

The important quantity is its surface normal, not just a point on the curve. The implicit gradient is proportional to (x³, z³). liquidSquircleNormal in src/glass-distortion.js combines that profile with the nearest XY boundary direction. The rim steepens near the outer edge and settles smoothly into the flat face.

The edge's blend uses a quintic curve. This exact expression is inside liquidEdgeMask:

float t = clamp(inside / width, 0.0, 1.0);
float eased = t * t * t * (t * (t * 6.0 - 15.0) + 10.0);
return clamp(1.0 - eased, 0.0, 1.0);

inside is distance inward from the boundary. At the outer edge, the mask is strongest. At the inner limit of the bevel, it is zero. The curve's first and second derivatives are zero at both ends, which avoids an abrupt join with the flat middle.

The WebGL path then uses this ray calculation from liquidLensOffset:

vec3 ray = refract(vec3(0.0, 0.0, -1.0), normal, 1.0 / max(ior, 1.001));
return ray.xy / max(-ray.z, 0.001) * thickness * 0.7 * edge * max(strength, 0.0);

The offset is applied to the backdrop texture coordinates. It is an image-space approximation of refraction through a rounded surface; there is no 3D mesh with a ray-traced volume behind every card. Thickness, depth, and distortion give useful control over that approximation.

Zero depth removes the bevel, and zero distortion disables its sampling strength. Small controls bound the bevel by their own dimensions so a flat center remains. The Z radius does not change the CSS corner radius: XY shape and depth profile are separate inputs.

Mirror at the boundary, then soften the result

The border reflection mirrors across the nearest local boundary, not across the center of the card. Top and bottom rims reverse the vertical direction, side rims reverse horizontally, and rounded corners follow their local boundary normal.

liquidReflectionProfile in src/glass-distortion.js first bounds the active strip and outward reach:

float band = min(width, min(thickness, padding * 0.3));
if (band <= 0.001 || inside >= band) return vec2(0.0);
float reach = min(thickness * 0.6, padding * 0.2);
return vec2(2.0 * inside + reach, liquidEdgeMask(inside, band));

The 2.0 * inside term crosses the boundary and reverses the normal axis. The extra reach samples a small amount of content beyond the pane. That is why text beneath a bottom edge can appear upside down in the rim.

The site captures 64 CSS pixels of padding around the lens. The reflection reach and its blur footprint are bounded within that available neighborhood. This prevents the approximation from asking for a large, uncaptured region beyond the card.

The maximum softening radius is calculated by the same bounded helper in GLSL and WGSL:

float liquidReflectionBlurRadius(float edgeBlend, float radius, float width, float padding) {
  float limit = min(max(width, 0.0) * 0.5, max(padding, 0.0) * 0.1);
  return min(max(radius, 0.0), limit) * clamp(edgeBlend, 0.0, 1.0);
}

A center-weighted five-tap kernel weights the center twice as much as each left, right, up, and down sample. The weights total six. Extra taps run only when a relevant rim sample has a nonzero radius; they do not add another full-screen blur pass.

This is still screen-space glass. A flat backdrop cannot reveal hidden objects or true environmental reflections. The mirrored rim can look convincing over text and shapes, but it is not a physically complete reflection model.

Keep hover and scrolling in the same coordinate system

Moving a canvas with CSS is not enough to move a lens correctly. If its texture coordinates stayed fixed, the sampled image would travel with the card, as though it were printed on the glass.

The hover path records the card's local plane. createGlassView in src/glass-view.js builds the projection and rotation that correspond to CSS perspective, lift, scale, and rotation. The shader projects backdrop coordinates into the card's current view. Its surface normals rotate too, so the rounded edge reacts to the angle.

The mirrored point is projected through that same transform. A nested lens samples its parent's already-projected canvas without projecting it twice. src/glass-backdrop-projection.js separately maps cached foreground and glass images into another lens's backdrop.

For scrolling, the scene is attached to the document. Page cards and their sampled coordinates move together in the browser. Fixed navigation needs updated scene positions as the document passes behind it, but its cached text images do not need a fresh asynchronous capture on every scroll event.

Foreground captures are refreshed for meaningful content or size changes. The captured fonts are embedded from the same local faces as the live page; otherwise the distorted text could have different glyph shapes or line breaks.

WebGL cards, WebGPU ribbons, useful fallbacks

Cards, badges, navigation, and the draggable lens use the adapted WebGL renderer in src/vendor/liquidglass.js. The two labs on this page use that renderer directly.

The landing-page artwork uses VGPU, which manages its WebGPU surface and WGSL effect in src/shader.js. It receives a backdrop sampler from the glass controller and the same root material. Its procedural ribbon boundary has a quartic bevel calculation and the shared reflection profile, but it is not the exact same fragment shader as a rounded rectangle.

The ribbon code samples a shifted red channel, a center green channel, and an oppositely shifted blue channel. Its shared rim softness combines with global blur in one sampling kernel. Zero distortion also gates its chromatic split. The ribbons are drawn back to front and tinted through the site's palette.

The ribbon path takes the shared frost, blur, distortion, chromatic, depth, reflection, and softness values. It derives its own bounded thickness and refraction offset; it does not run the card shader's GLSL refract calculation or its refractive-index control. Sharing a material does not make the two geometry models identical.

The site initializes that renderer only at widths of at least 781px, with GPU capability available. At mobile sizes the artwork is hidden, without reserving a confusing strip of empty space. If setup fails at desktop size, static CSS artwork remains. If the WebGL glass cannot initialize, the native frosted CSS treatment remains available.

The text, CV content, and anchors are static HTML. They remain useful when scripting or GPU features are unavailable. GPU support changes the visual layer, rather than whether somebody can read the page.

What the effect costs

There are two main costs: creating and uploading scene images, and sampling them in the shader. I keep those concerns separate:

  • Cache foreground images. src/glass-backdrop.js queues captures with limited concurrency and refreshes affected content. Scrolling repositions cached images rather than recapturing every frame.
  • Avoid needless blur passes. At zero full-surface blur, both background samplers use the sharp texture. Positive blur keeps the renderer's horizontal/vertical passes. Rim softness adds texture taps only in its active band.
  • Bound resolution and motion. Card glass is capped at one pixel per CSS pixel while live text retains native browser resolution. The ribbon surface is capped at 1.5 device pixel ratio and its loop at 30 FPS. The pixel background paints at up to 12 FPS.
  • Render when something changes. The glass scheduler batches geometry and scene updates. Scroll and drag can flush immediately; hidden pages cancel pending scheduled work, and the ribbon loop pauses when hidden or outside the viewport.
  • Respect motion preference. The CV's motion setting and operating-system reduced-motion preference keep animated parts still. These article labs start with a static scene and redraw for controls and layout changes; they do not need an idle animation loop.

The vendor's WebGL context-loss handlers skip GPU draws while the context is lost. Restoration rebuilds programs, buffers, and framebuffer state; the next requested render can repopulate the images. Live HTML remains available throughout. That does not mean context loss automatically switches the production page to CSS glass—the initialization fallback and context-restoration path are different mechanisms. The labs expose an explicit fallback status if their GPU path becomes unavailable.

These are implementation choices, not a benchmark. A device's shader throughput, capture sizes, and number of overlapping lenses still matter. More chromatic or blurred samples cost work even when they use an existing texture.

Reproduce the important pieces

I would trace the implementation in this order:

  1. Start with one ordinary HTML card and a background canvas. Keep its content outside the distorted image.
  2. Establish a shared material and a padded backdrop crop before adding more lenses.
  3. Use a boundary-distance field, a smooth rim mask, and a surface normal to change sample positions only near the edges.
  4. Add the bounded boundary mirror, then per-channel offsets and rim softness. Test zero values independently.
  5. Match sample coordinates to scrolling and hover transforms before adding nested surfaces.
  6. Add cached foreground images when an overlay must see text. Keep the original text in the DOM.
  7. Keep a CSS fallback and a disposal path for observers, GPU resources, and scheduled frames.

The parameter lab isolates steps 2–4. The layer lab makes step 6 visible with a small, explicitly composited source scene. Fullscreen enlarges the same lab; it does not switch to a different renderer.

Source map and further reading

These file and function names refer to this project's source tree. The editable repository is private; I have included the relevant small excerpts above so this article does not depend on access to it.

Source path Follow this responsibility
src/main.js Async startup, motion preference, desktop ribbon lifecycle.
src/liquid-glass.js createGlassSurfaces, shared material and scene, output beneath live content.
src/glass-backdrop.js createGlassBackdrop, capture queue and compareBackdropLayers.
src/glass-settings.js and src/glass.css Main material inputs, normalized values, clear variant, CSS fallback.
src/glass-distortion.js liquidEdgeMask, liquidSquircleNormal, liquidLensOffset, reflection profile and radius.
src/vendor/liquidglass.js GlassRenderer, uploadAndBlur, renderGlassPanel, GLSL material and context handlers.
src/glass-view.js and src/glass-geometry.js Local planes, hover projection, document/viewport coordinates.
src/glass-backdrop-projection.js Sampling tilted foreground and glass layers.
src/shader.js The separate VGPU/WGSL ribbon effect and lifecycle.
src/blog/demos.js This article's isolated lab setup and controlled scene composition.

The upstream liquidglass repository documents the renderer this local implementation adapts. VGPU documents the WebGPU tooling used for the landing-page artwork. MDN's backdrop-filter reference and Fullscreen API guide explain the browser features used by the fallback and labs.

The site's third-party notices retain the renderer and bundled html-to-image attribution and licenses. The labs reuse that local renderer; they do not claim to replace its upstream authorship.
